messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Layla still remembers the morning the shelling began. She was 32, a prosecutor in her home city, when the war reached her neighbourhood. She had stayed in her apartment against orders, believing she would be safe. Then the voices came—men shouting in Arabic, boots on the stairs, pounding on doors. She hid in the bathroom, convinced they were tracking her, that someone was watching from the window across the street. For twelve hours she did not move, listening to the sounds of forced entry and gunfire two floors down. She escaped the city three days later, and eventually resettled in the United States with her husband. But the feeling of being followed never fully left her.

Now, at 44, Layla works as a prosecutor in a busy district attorney's office. The courthouse hallways are long and crowded, and every time someone walks behind her for more than a few steps, her chest tightens and she has to glance over her shoulder. She tells herself it is irrational—she is safe here—but the sensation is immediate and physical. A colleague's voice that carries an accent similar to the men that day can make her heart pound for minutes afterward; she will excuse herself to the restroom and stand with her back to the wall until the alarm fades. The courtroom itself is worse. From the prosecutor's table she feels the eyes of the gallery, the judge, the defendant—watched, observed, pinned in place. She has started to sit with her back to the wall even in meetings, and she wakes most nights at 3 a.m. to walk through her apartment and check that all the doors are locked, sometimes twice.

This hypervigilance has reshaped how Layla sees herself and the world. She used to describe herself as a happy person, but now she says she is always miserable, hollowed out by a constant low dread. The smallest disruption—a dropped stack of files, a raised voice in chambers—leaves her feeling as though she cannot handle anything at all. She has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous, that no place is truly safe except her own home, and even that only partially. It is not a thought she voices aloud; it is the quiet assumption beneath every decision she makes.

The more she scans for threats, the more she finds them. Her vigilance sharpens her awareness of sounds—the unexpected slam of a door, a car backfiring on the street—and each time her body responds before her mind can catch up. That reaction, in turn, confirms that danger is near, and she begins to listen more intently, to watch more closely, and to feel even more certain that someone is tracking her movements. She has stopped taking the subway because the tunnels feel too enclosed and the crowds too anonymous; she drives a route that avoids any street where she once had a startle response. At work she asks for an office with a door she can lock, and during trial breaks she sits in the small windowless conference room rather than the attorneys' lounge, because there are fewer people to watch her.

Her husband has noticed the change. He asks why she no longer wants to go to the grocery store or eat at restaurants. Layla tells him she is tired, but the truth is she can only feel safe in the apartment, and even then she checks the locks twice before bed. The brief periods of calm she finds at home have begun to shrink; a loud motorcycle outside or a neighbour's raised voice can shatter them for hours. She used to take pride in her ability to stay composed in court, but now she dreads each hearing, sure she will be exposed as someone who cannot cope.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the hallway last week. A defendant she had convicted years ago was released on parole, and she saw him across the lobby. He did not approach her, but the instant she recognised his face, she felt a surge of terror so acute she had to lean against the wall. She was certain he was watching her, that he had followed her into the building, that she was about to be cornered again. It took her ten minutes to breathe normally. She knew, rationally, that he had no reason to target her. But the feeling did not listen to reason. That night she told her husband she needed to talk to someone, and she made an appointment. She is most afraid that she will never feel safe again, that her career—the one thing she has rebuilt from scratch—will be destroyed by the very vigilance that once kept her alive.
